description: We are JARFYN FIRE, a team of six university students studying Software, Systems, and Industrial Engineering. Participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to develop an innovative solution for harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS hotspot data. Combining technology, data analysis, and creativity, we strive to turn satellite data into meaningful insights for better environmental monitoring. Our team is complete, and we are ready to collaborate, learn, and make an impact!
summary:
NASA's two fire sensors disagree: VIIRS sees 5–12 times more hot spots than MODIS, and simply joining them makes global fire appear to grow by +446%, an artifact, not a real trend.
  IgniVision harmonizes 23 years of NASA FIRMS hot spots (2003–2025) from MODIS and VIIRS into a single series: a per-country, per-month factor plus an XGBoost corrector, learned on their 2012–2021 overlap at 0.25° × month (R² = 0.887, +1.3% bias on the unseen year 2023). With it, the global decline in fire is weaker than MODIS alone suggests (−9.0% instead of −11.7% per decade) and 89 of 132 countries look worse.
  What makes IgniVision different is the climate link. A warming climate brings more fire weather (IPCC AR6), and fires release greenhouse gases that warm it further. So from the same harmonized hot spots we turn fire energy into burned biomass and greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, N2O) for Peru's 25 departments, month by month; they track NASA burned area (r = 0.92 per year) and stay within ~4% of GFED5.1. A web app lets anyone pick a place, read a burn and emissions calendar with anomalies and alerts, and download the data.
details:
Live app: https://boisterous-semolina-93a764.netlify.app/

Project files (data, code, papers): https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/17tO-Wod20W4CUxRCV37SFB0BPkMQCba_

What it does

IgniVision turns NASA's two incompatible fire records, MODIS and VIIRS, into one consistent record, derives greenhouse-gas emissions from the same hot spots, and makes both explorable in a web app.

1. Official data curation. NASA FIRMS standard-processing data only: MODIS Aqua (2003–2023) and a canonical VIIRS series (Suomi NPP from 20 Jan 2012, NOAA-20 from 1 Apr 2018, NOAA-21 only to fill official gaps). Local files were verified byte by byte against the FIRMS server. No hot spot is deleted: low confidence, type and official missing days are flags. 63.9 M MODIS and 282.6 M VIIRS detections worldwide.

2. Harmonization by statistical intercalibration. Using days observed by both sensors in 2012–2021, we learn how many hot spots VIIRS would have seen for each MODIS Aqua observation: a per-country × calendar-month factor plus an XGBoost Poisson corrector (GPU) with neighbouring cells, previous month, day/night split, FRP and fire-size mix. Applied to 2003–2011, it gives a homogeneous 0.25° × month global series for 2003–2025.

3. Validation and uncertainty. Test year 2023: R² 0.887 per cell, +1.3% bias (factor only: 0.839). Leave-one-year-out validation. "Travel to the past" (calibrate 2018–2023, predict 2012–2017): R² 0.873, +2.0% bias. Conformal bands per cell and an error-by-zone-size table (±12% for zones with more than 10,000 hot spots). Cross-check with GFED5.1: emissions scale with harmonized hot spots (elasticity 1.03 ± 0.02, 134 countries) with only a small jump in 2012 (+4.5% ± 2.3 after trend; placebo cuts −2.4% to +2.0%).

4. What makes it different: the climate link. A warming climate is increasing fire weather in many regions (IPCC AR6), and fires release CO2, CH4 and N2O that add to warming. Measuring this loop needs a consistent fire record, so from the same harmonized hot spots IgniVision estimates greenhouse gases for Peru's 25 departments, month by month, 2003–2025.

• Fires: hot spots within 1 km on the same or consecutive days (687,777 fires).

• Biomass: fire radiative energy = sum of FRP × 43,200 s; burned biomass = energy × 0.368 kg/MJ (Wooster et al. 2005). For 2003–2011, Aqua energy is scaled to VIIRS with a per-month ratio learned in 2012–2021 (tested on 2022–2023: −4.4% and +2.0%).

• Gases: biomass × Andreae (2019) emission factors by biome; CO2e = CO2 + 27 CH4 + 273 N2O (IPCC AR6).

• Three layers: all detected fires (a minimum), fires confirmed by MODIS burned area MCD64A1, and a biome-corrected best estimate.

• Validation: 64% of MCD64A1 burned area (2012–2023) has a VIIRS fire within ~0.9 km and 4 days (4% by chance); r = 0.92 per year and 0.80 across departments; same fire season (Aug–Sep: 62% of burned area, 65% of CO2e). Corrected CO2e is within +0.4% (2003–2011) and −4.1% (2018–2022) of GFED5.1, both outside the calibration years. About 46% of INDECI and MINAM fire records match a detected fire within 10 km and 3 days after removing chance.

5. IgniVision web app. Pick the whole world, a country, a Peruvian department, or draw a circle, rectangle or freehand area; choose a period with a range slider; switch the source (Harmonized, MODIS, VIIRS). It shows a 3D globe with the Aqua, S-NPP and NOAA-20 satellites, a burn calendar by day, week, month or year (counts or anomaly vs. normal), a greenhouse-gas panel (CO2e, CO2, CH4, N2O; corrected, all detected or confirmed), early alerts (unusual increase, concentration, unusual year) and data downloads.

Benefits and intended impact

• Long fire trends without sensor jumps as MODIS retires, instead of restarting baselines in 2012.

• The diagnosis changes: the global decline in fire is −9.0% instead of −11.7% per decade; 89 of 132 countries look worse; India's increase becomes significant (+14.9% per decade); 2024 is a 23-year record for Bolivia, DR Congo, Angola and Venezuela.

• It warns against naive splicing (+446%), a real risk as national programs and Copernicus GFAS change sensors.

• Fire emissions that can be followed over time and place: monthly CO2, CH4 and N2O per Peruvian department (34.4 Mt CO2e in 2019, best estimate), cross-checked with NASA burned area, GFED5.1 and official records.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Python 3.13 (polars, pandas, numpy, pyarrow, scipy, shapely, scikit-learn, statsmodels, XGBoost 3.4 CUDA, PyTorch 2.13 CUDA, pyhdf, paramiko, matplotlib); JavaScript with D3.js 7.9, three.js 0.160 and TopoJSON, tested with Playwright; Parquet partitioned by year; a Windows laptop with an NVIDIA RTX 3050 GPU and a Linux laptop; Claude Code as AI coding assistant.

How it is creative

• We calibrate whole fire regimes by place and season instead of matching fires one by one (simultaneous passes happen on only ~5% of days).

• Fire-size mix as a variable halves the error where MODIS misses small burns (e.g. Spain, Thailand).

• "Travel to the past" validation tests the method the way it is used.

• Error bands depend on the size of the area the user draws.

• Greenhouse gases come from the same harmonized hot spots, with three honest layers (minimum, confirmed, corrected).

Factors the team considered

• Overpass time: Terra excluded (passes ~3 h earlier); Aqua orbital drift after 2022, so 2023 is the last year used.

• Official missing days and the VIIRS start date (20 Jan 2012).

• Industrial and gas-flare detections: type = 0 filter is mandatory outside Peru.

• No year or overpass time as model inputs (they memorize or worsen results).

• Limits: ~13 countries with little vegetation fire still fail; converted years carry ±10–20% uncertainty; 2003–2011 gives counts per cell, not individual hot spots. Gases: hot spots miss small, cloud-covered and understory fires; the biome correction is calibrated on GFED5.1, which also uses MODIS; biome is assigned per department; MCD64A1 confirmation ends in 2023. Our data do not prove that warming increases fire; that link comes from IPCC AR6.

• Accessibility (colorblind-safe palettes, bilingual interface) and NASA data as the core input.
